hints: Focus on what effervescence tells you when any acid is added to a carbonate mixture.
Remember that all common chlorides are soluble in water, so neither calcium chloride nor magnesium chloride can be the white solid Y.
Compare the solubilities of the two sulfates formed with sulfuric acid, only one of them is sparingly soluble and appears as a white precipitate.
walkthrough:
**Explain the effervescence**

Both magnesium carbonate and calcium carbonate react with acids to release carbon dioxide gas. That is why you see fizzing whatever acid you use.

$$\text{MCO}_3 + 2\text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{M}^{2+} + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Rule out the chloride options**

Hydrochloric acid would make $\text{CaCl}_2$ and $\text{MgCl}_2$. Both Group 2 chlorides are very soluble in water, so they stay in solution as colourless solutions.

No white solid could form, so options with hydrochloric acid cannot be right.

**Check the sulfate options**

Sulfuric acid would make $\text{CaSO}_4$ and $\text{MgSO}_4$. Here solubility is the key difference.

$$\text{CaCO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{CaSO}_4 + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Identify the white solid Y**

Calcium sulfate is sparingly soluble, so it appears as a white solid or precipitate. Magnesium sulfate is soluble, so it stays dissolved.

Therefore the only combination that gives both effervescence and a white solid is sulfuric acid with calcium sulfate.

options.A: Hydrochloric acid does give effervescence with carbonates, but calcium chloride is soluble in water. It would form a colourless solution, not a white solid Y.
options.B: Hydrochloric acid does give effervescence, but magnesium chloride is also soluble in water. Like all common chlorides, it stays in solution and cannot be the observed white solid.
options.C: Sulfuric acid reacts with both carbonates to give CO2 effervescence. Calcium sulfate formed is sparingly soluble and is seen as the white solid Y, while magnesium sulfate stays in solution.
options.D: Sulfuric acid is the correct type of reagent, but magnesium sulfate is soluble in water. It would not appear as a white solid, so this pairing does not fit the observation.
